expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Distinguishing Cultural Discourse Norms From Oppositional Behavior
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A newly enrolled seventh grader experiencing housing instability uses lively overlapping banter common in his home community during group work and looks down when corrected. After three verbal clashes in two weeks, a teacher requests immediate transfer to a self-contained EBD unit for "oppositional defiant disorder."
expandableCase.diagnosis: Avoid informal clinical labels, examine cultural and contextual setting events, and teach norms using least-intensive non-coercive supports.
expandableCase.explanation: Educators must not diagnose psychiatric disorders or misinterpret culturally grounded discourse and ecological stressors as EBD. Applying preventive, culturally responsive instruction and equitable disciplinary safeguards addresses classroom expectations without coercive escalation or premature restrictive placement.

expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Balancing Trauma Setting Events, Function, and Clinical Referral
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A ninth grader with Emotional Disturbance and a documented trauma history bolts from English whenever cold-called to read aloud, muttering that he is worthless and disclosing recurring nightmares and passive hopelessness. Staff label his exits "manipulative" and propose public privilege revocation.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Use label-free ABC data to address escape triggers privately, eliminate shaming, and make a scope-bound referral for mental health screening.
expandableCase.explanation: Trauma history acts as a critical setting event that intensifies perceived threat, yet effective intervention still requires label-free functional analysis of immediate classroom escape triggers. Avoiding public humiliation protects dignity while referring acute internalizing distress to qualified school clinicians.

expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Protecting LRE Rigor Against Unilateral Removal After Outbursts
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: Following two loud verbal outbursts during tenth-grade Algebra, an administrator proposes moving a student with EBD from his co-taught class to an isolated online credit-recovery room with simplified packets. The student holds a 78% quiz average, and the IEP team has not reviewed or revised his BIP.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Prevent unilateral placement removal, convene the IEP team to revise data-backed BIP supports in Algebra, and maintain grade-level rigor.
expandableCase.explanation: IDEA prohibits unilateral placement changes outside the IEP process and requires exhausting supplementary aids and function-based plan revisions before moving to a more restrictive setting. Preserving high-expectation curriculum equity honors the student's academic capability and LRE entitlement.

expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Preserving Communication Access Through Functional Communication Training
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: An eighth grader with EBD and pragmatic language deficits swears at teachers when stuck on multi-step writing prompts. Staff respond by confiscating his speech-to-text tablet as a consequence and demanding silent compliance before he may request help, causing work refusal to triple across classes.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Preserve uninterrupted assistive tool access and implement FCT to teach, reinforce, and generalize respectful help and break requests.
expandableCase.explanation: Revoking communication or writing accommodations as punishment violates access rights and strips away the very tool that lowers frustration. Functional Communication Training replaces profanity with a socially acceptable, functionally equivalent request reinforced across teachers without coercive demands.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A student escapes difficult work by yelling and already responds to a visual cue. Which replacement communication should be taught first?

Allow open-ended dismissal from every difficult assignment whenever frustration signals first appear.
Teach a brief, accessible help or break request that earns a prompt reply and a planned return to task.
Teach the student to deliver a verbal apology after leaving the classroom and returning from the hallway.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: A functionally equivalent request must be easier and more efficient than the problem behavior while still preserving instruction. Prompt reinforcement followed by a supported return makes the replacement usable and sustainable.

Assign enjoyable solitary recreation routines so the student avoids the stress of approaching peer groups.

Teach when and how to request the accommodation, rehearse across partners, honor requests, and track independence.

expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Fading Prompt Dependence With Private Self-Monitoring Logs
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: An eleventh grader with EBD stays on task 85% of the period when a paraprofessional sits beside him giving constant verbal prompts, yet drops to 20% and shuts down whenever the adult steps away or deducts points on a front whiteboard for off-task moments.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Fade adult proximity systematically using task-analyzed checklists, a private self-monitoring log, and DRO or DRA for independent intervals.
expandableCase.explanation: Continuous one-to-one adult prompting breeds prompt dependence and adolescent stigma, while public punitive point loss triggers withdrawal and resentment. Pairing structured task analysis with age-dignified private self-monitoring and differential reinforcement transfers behavioral control to the learner.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A student will self-monitor on-task behavior during independent work. What should the teacher establish before using a timer and checklist?
choices: Use a broad verbal reminder to behave well and accept every self-recorded tally mark without verification.
Display the student’s self-monitoring tally chart publicly on the wall so classmates can double-check marks.
Track final assignment grades in place of accuracy checks because self-monitoring needs no direct validation.
Define target actions observably, teach the recording routine, and periodically check agreement directly.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: An observable definition and explicit practice make self-recording teachable. Occasional comparison with direct observation checks accuracy while preserving the student ownership that can support independence.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A student can list coping strategies but does not select one when early tension appears. Which instruction is most likely to improve use?

Assign one standard calming routine for every school setting without asking for the student’s preferences.
Reinforce reciting emotion vocabulary on flashcards without rehearsing an actionable coping response.
Wait for a peak crisis episode and introduce several brand-new coping options while tension is highest.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Strategy knowledge alone does not ensure timely use. Teaching antecedent cues, choice, calm rehearsal, and supported application builds fluency before high-intensity moments and provides evidence about which response works.

Complete any skipped morning organization steps quietly for the student without recording adult support.
Deliver step-by-step adult verbal prompts every morning indefinitely so arrival errors stay rare.

Co-create a realistic target, graph private data, review patterns together, and choose the next adjustment.
Post the student’s daily call-out graph beside the classroom door to strengthen public accountability.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A school is considering check-in/check-out for a student with inconsistent morning engagement. What should determine whether it is appropriate?
choices: Enroll the student in check-in/check-out because every learner with EBD should participate in Tier 2 routines.
Launch the daily check-in sheet without defining measurable targets and keep it running through spring.
Discontinue existing individualized IEP supports once the standard Tier 2 check-in routine begins.

expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A school team considers Emotional Disturbance eligibility for a fifth-grade bilingual student based solely on one teacher rating scale (T-score 74) and informal remarks shared in the staff lounge. expandableCase.explanation: IDEA prohibits basing eligibility on any single measure or source and requires nondiscriminatory assessment across settings, informants, and languages. diagrams.title: Multi-Tiered PBIS & Classroom Prevention Architecture

Third, Tier 2 targeted supports layer rapid, structured interventions—such as Check-In/Check-Out (CICO), daily behavior report cards, and small-group social-skills instruction—on top of Tier 1. Fourth, students with intensive, persistent needs receive Tier 3 individualized supports combining FBA-driven Behavior Intervention Plans with family-centered mental-health wraparound. Finally, ongoing fidelity and outcome monitoring guides fading or intensification across tiers.

diagrams.title: Acting-Out Cycle & Safe Nonviolent De-Escalation Pathway
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Match staff responses to each phase of Colvin’s acting-out cycle—from calm prevention and early de-escalation through peak safety protocols to recovery and restorative debriefing.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow aligning nonviolent crisis prevention, verbal de-escalation, safety-first peak protocols, and restorative recovery across the acting-out cycle.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right acting-out cycle flow from calm prevention and trigger management through agitation and acceleration de-escalation and peak safety to recovery and restorative repair.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right across the acting-out cycle. First, during Calm and Trigger phases, educators teach coping routines, maintain structure, and address school or nonschool triggers proactively before arousal rises. Second, during Agitation, staff notice early behavioral cues (pacing, withdrawal, darting gaze) and offer calm empathy, reduced demands, structured choices, or a practiced cool-down break. Third, during Acceleration, staff avoid power struggles and rapid lecturing, instead using a low calm tone, physical space, concise neutral prompts, and clear wait time. Fourth, at Peak, safety is the sole priority: clear bystanders, follow the individualized crisis plan, and avoid punitive escalation or prohibited restraint/seclusion except under strict imminent-harm law and policy. Finally, during De-escalation and Recovery, allow physiological regulation, assign a low-demand re-entry task, and hold a calm restorative debriefing only once fully regulated.
textEquivalent: Calm & Trigger Prevention: Build predictable routines, teach and rehearse self-calming signals during calm periods, and buffer known academic, sensory, or interpersonal triggers proactively.

Agitation Phase — Early Supportive Interruption: Recognize subtle early warning cues (fidgeting, withdrawal, vocal tension) and intervene quietly with validation, independent break options, or manageable choices.

Acceleration Phase — Nonviolent Verbal De-Escalation: Eliminate power struggles and audience pressure; use calm neutral voice, respectful distance, minimal words, and dignified exit options with wait time.

Peak Phase — Safety-First Crisis Protocol: Prioritize immediate physical safety of the student and peers, clear the environment, follow the written crisis plan, and never lecture or punish during peak distress; restrict emergency physical interventions strictly to imminent serious physical harm per law and trained protocol.

De-Escalation, Recovery & Restorative Repair: Permit quiet physiological recovery, re-engage with an easy familiar task, and conduct non-shaming problem-solving and relationship repair only after the student returns to baseline calm.

nodes.detail: Step out of power struggles: lower vocal volume, increase personal space, remove peer audience, give one brief neutral direction, and allow silent processing time.

nodes.label: Peak: Safety Protocol Without Escalation
nodes.detail: Focus exclusively on physical safety—clear peers and hazards, summon trained crisis support per IEP/crisis plan, avoid arguing or punitive escalation, and observe strict legal limits on restraint/seclusion.

nodes.label: Recovery, Debriefing & Restorative Repair
nodes.detail: Allow physiological cool-down and low-demand re-entry first; once baseline calm returns, conduct brief restorative debriefing and update antecedent supports to prevent recurrence.

diagrams.title: Direct Behavioral Observation, IOA Verification & Multi-Source Triangulation
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Ensure defensible EBD assessment by pairing reliability, validity, and cultural fairness standards with dimension-matched direct observation recording, interobserver agreement checks, multi-source triangulation, and confidential instructional action.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow connecting psychometric and cultural fairness, matched direct observation metrics, IOA verification, multi-source triangulation, and confidential instructional links.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right assessment flow from psychometric and cultural fairness through dimension-matched direct observation, interobserver agreement checks, and multi-source triangulation to confidential assessment-to-instruction links.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, teams verify reliability, validity, and cultural and linguistic fairness across all tools, rejecting single-score decisions under nondiscriminatory evaluation safeguards. Second, observers match the direct behavioral recording method to the behavior dimension—frequency or rate for discrete countable events, duration for continuous episodes, latency for time to start after a cue, and partial, whole, or momentary interval sampling for high-rate or continuous behaviors. Third, teams safeguard data accuracy using clear operational definitions, interobserver agreement (IOA) checks, and observer-bias controls across multiple settings. diagrams.title: Functional Behavior Assessment (FBA) & Replacement-Skill Engineering Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Move systematically from an observable behavior definition and ABC/scatter-plot observations to a four-function hypothesis, competing-behavior pathway, and thinned reinforcement schedule.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow mapping FBA observation and four-function analysis onto competing-behavior replacement-skill engineering and reinforcement schedules.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right FBA flow from observable definition through direct ABC and scatter-plot data and four-function hypothesis to competing-behavior pathway and reinforcement schedules.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the team defines the target behavior in concrete, observable, measurable terms (topography, frequency, duration, intensity). Second, observers gather direct ABC records, scatter plots, and structured interviews to identify setting events, immediate antecedents, and maintaining consequences across routines. Third, the team synthesizes data into a testable functional hypothesis identifying whether the behavior is maintained by escape/avoidance, attention, tangible/activity access, or sensory regulation. Fourth, the team constructs a competing-behavior pathway that neutralizes triggers, teaches an efficient functionally equivalent replacement behavior (FERB), and moves toward the long-term desired behavior. Finally, staff implement differential reinforcement (DRA/DRI/DRO), withhold inadvertent reinforcement of problem behavior safely, and systematically thin schedules as the replacement skill generalizes.
textEquivalent: Observable & Measurable Behavior Definition: Specify exactly what the behavior looks and sounds like so multiple staff record consistent baseline frequency, duration, latency, or intensity.

Direct ABC, Scatter-Plot & Interview Data: Combine direct antecedent-behavior-consequence observations, time-of-day scatter plots, and student/staff interviews to expose setting events, triggers, and immediate payoffs.

Four-Function Hypothesis Formulation: Determine whether behavior primarily serves escape/avoidance (task or social demand), attention (adult or peer), access to tangibles/activities, or automatic sensory regulation.

Competing-Behavior Pathway & FERB Design: Pair antecedent adjustments with a functionally equivalent replacement behavior (FERB) that requires less effort and delivers the same function faster than the problem behavior.

Differential Reinforcement & Schedule Thinning: Reinforce the replacement behavior immediately on a dense schedule (DRA/DRI), minimize accidental payoff for the target behavior, and gradually thin reinforcement toward natural classroom contingencies.

diagrams.title: IDEA Disciplinary Protections & Manifestation Determination Review (MDR) Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Apply IDEA §300.530 disciplinary safeguards—tracking the 10-day removal threshold, conducting the two-question MDR, distinguishing manifestation outcomes from special-circumstances IAES, and protecting continued FAPE.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow outlining IDEA §300.530 disciplinary change-of-placement rules, Manifestation Determination Review (MDR), special circumstances, and FAPE continuity.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right IDEA discipline flow from 10-day disciplinary change-of-placement threshold through two-prong MDR review to manifestation FBA/BIP return or special-circumstances IAES and continued FAPE.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, schools monitor disciplinary removals; exceeding 10 consecutive school days—or a pattern of cumulative removals over 10 days in a school year—constitutes a disciplinary change of placement requiring immediate procedural safeguards notice. Second, within 10 school days of that decision, the LEA, parent, and relevant IEP team members conduct a Manifestation Determination Review (MDR) answering two questions: whether the conduct was caused by or had a direct and substantial relationship to the disability, or whether it was the direct result of the LEA’s failure to implement the IEP. Third, if either prong is yes (a manifestation), the team conducts an FBA and implements or revises a BIP, remedies any IEP implementation failure immediately, and returns the student to the agreed placement unless the parent agrees otherwise or a special circumstance applies. Fourth, only three special circumstances—weapons, illegal drugs/controlled substances, or serious bodily injury at school—permit unilateral removal to an Interim Alternative Educational Setting (IAES) for up to 45 school days regardless of manifestation. Finally, whenever removals exceed 10 school days, the student must continue receiving FAPE services to progress in the general curriculum and toward IEP goals.

If Manifestation — FBA/BIP & Return to Placement: Conduct an FBA and implement or review/modify a BIP, fix any IEP implementation gap immediately, and return the student to the prior placement unless parent and LEA agree to a change.

Non-Manifestation or 45-Day Special-Circumstances IAES: If not a manifestation, general disciplinary procedures apply (with continued FAPE); for weapons, illegal drugs, or serious bodily injury at school, the LEA may use an IAES for up to 45 school days regardless of manifestation.

Continued FAPE & Dispute-Resolution Protections: Beyond 10 removal days, the IEP team ensures ongoing educational services enabling general-curriculum participation and IEP goal progress, alongside expedited due-process appeal rights.

diagrams.title: Social-Emotional Learning (SEL), Cognitive-Behavioral Self-Regulation & Family-Agency Wraparound Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Connect explicit SEL and cognitive-behavioral self-regulation instruction to self-monitoring generalization, collaborative family-agency wraparound, and ethical confidentiality and mandatory-reporting duties.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow linking explicit SEL and CBT self-regulation coaching with generalization cues, family-mental-health wraparound, and ethical confidentiality boundaries.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right SEL and wraparound flow from explicit emotion-regulation and CBT problem-solving through self-monitoring and caregiver-agency wraparound to ethical confidentiality and mandatory reporting.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, educators explicitly teach social-emotional learning and cognitive-behavioral self-regulation—emotion recognition, physiological stress cues, cognitive reframing, and step-by-step social problem-solving. Second, learners practice self-monitoring, self-instruction, and discreet classroom generalization cues so coping strategies transfer into general education, hallways, and peer settings. Third, school teams partner with families as co-designers, aligning home and school strengths, cultural values, and communication routines. Fourth, with informed written consent, educators coordinate school-based and community mental-health wraparound services so behavioral and clinical supports reinforce one another. Finally, practitioners uphold FERPA confidentiality, scope-of-practice boundaries (educators do not diagnose or prescribe medication), and statutory mandatory reporting when abuse, neglect, or imminent self-harm/harm-to-others arises.

Culturally Responsive Caregiver Partnership: Engage families proactively with strengths-first communication, shared goal setting, and nonjudgmental problem-solving rather than contacting caregivers only after disciplinary incidents.

Mental-Health & Agency Wraparound Coordination: With signed release of information, align school behavioral supports with counselors, school psychologists, and community mental-health providers around unified wraparound goals.

Ethical Confidentiality, Scope & Mandatory Reporting: Protect educational and behavioral records under FERPA, stay within educator scope (never recommending medication changes), and execute immediate mandatory reporting and safety protocols when abuse, neglect, or imminent harm is disclosed.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Separate Escape and Attention Functions Across Morning and Afternoon Routines
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Analyze scatterplot and direct ABC data for a fifth-grade student with EBD to formulate separate functional hypotheses, address biological/home setting events, and replace a failing one-size-fits-all point-loss system.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Caleb (Grade 5, EBD) loses points under one response-cost chart all day. Ten days of ABC and scatterplot data reveal two patterns: at 9:15 AM independent writing, paper-tearing and chair-tipping occur 8 of 10 days—peaking Mondays and Thursdays after late caregiver shifts and skipped breakfast—ending in hallway removal. At 1:30 PM hallway and art transitions, loud teasing draws peer laughter and 45-second teacher lectures.
taskParts: Write two separate, observable competing-behavior functional statements distinguishing the 9:15 AM setting-event/escape chain from the 1:30 PM peer-and-adult attention chain.
Explain why the single response-cost point-loss chart fails in both contexts and how hallway removals and 45-second lectures inadvertently maintain the problem behaviors.
Recommend distinct, function-matched antecedent, teaching, and consequence strategies for morning writing and afternoon transitions.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Separate the 9:15 AM cluster (skipped breakfast/fatigue setting events, independent writing trigger, hallway-removal escape) from the 1:30 PM cluster (unstructured transition trigger, peer laughter and 45-second lecture attention).

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply functional behavioral assessment principles (setting events, antecedents, behavior, maintaining consequences), competing-behavior pathways, and WWC elementary behavioral intervention evidence.

planningFrame.label: Intervention plan
planningFrame.guidance: Neutralize morning setting events (breakfast check-in, chunked writing starters, earned help/break pass) while redesigning afternoon transitions (structured helper role, brief neutral cues, peer-earned recognition).

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Track morning and afternoon rates separately on daily behavioral logs, verify adult fidelity on eliminating 45-second lectures and hallway removals, and partner nonjudgmentally with caregivers.

successCriteria: Explicitly distinguishes two separate behavioral functions—morning task escape compounded by fatigue/hunger setting events vs. afternoon peer and adult attention.
Explains the exact reinforcement traps: hallway removal negatively reinforces morning tearing, while 45-second lectures positively reinforce afternoon teasing.
Proposes setting-event neutralization (non-stigmatizing breakfast access and Monday/Thursday soft check-in) alongside separate morning and afternoon replacement behaviors.
Specifies separate period-by-period data tracking so progress in one routine is not masked by totals from the other.
commonPitfalls: Assigning a single global function ("Caleb wants control") across both morning writing and afternoon transitions.
Ignoring the Monday/Thursday sleep and nutrition setting events or blaming caregivers instead of building dignified school check-in supports.
Keeping hallway removals or lengthy verbal lectures in place while simply raising the point-loss penalty.
Averaging morning and afternoon incident counts into one daily score that obscures whether each function-specific strategy is working.
sampleOutline: Dual functional hypotheses: Morning paper-tearing and chair-tipping are maintained by escape from independent writing (amplified by Monday/Thursday fatigue and skipped breakfast); afternoon teasing is maintained by peer laughter and adult lecture attention.
Reinforcement-trap audit: Uniform point loss teaches no replacement skill, hallway removals reward escape, and 45-second reprimands deliver rich attention.

Matched morning & afternoon plans: Offer a discreet breakfast Check-In, sentence frames, and a break/help card at 9:15 AM; assign a structured transition leadership role, pre-correct expectations, minimize reprimands to 5-second neutral prompts, and build positive peer recognition at 1:30 PM.
Disaggregated monitoring: Graph morning escape episodes, afternoon attention episodes, and replacement-skill usage separately with weekly fidelity reviews.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Engineer an FCT and Differential Reinforcement Plan for Escape-Maintained Math Disruption
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Design a function-matched replacement teaching and differential reinforcement plan for a fourth-grade student whose math-block profanity and throwing are maintained by task escape.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Brianna (Grade 4, EBD) yells profanity and sweeps fraction tiles off her desk during timed independent math work (6 episodes weekly). A completed FBA confirmed escape from multi-step fraction tasks and slow help access (4-minute average wait). Her current plan uses verbal reprimands and losing Friday free time, yet weekly disruptions rose from 4 to 6 over a month and she completes fewer than 20% of assigned problems.
taskParts: Design a Functional Communication Training (FCT) protocol specifying an explicit, low-effort replacement request (help or brief break) that produces faster, more reliable reinforcement than yelling or throwing tiles.
Integrate Differential Reinforcement of Alternative Behavior (DRA) and Incompatible Behavior (DRI) with extinction of escape-maintained disruption and antecedent math supports.
Map out a systematic schedule-thinning plan so Brianna transitions from immediate dense reinforcement to realistic classroom wait times and sustained independent math completion.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Center the plan on the verified escape function, the 4-minute teacher wait barrier, the spike from 4 to 6 weekly episodes under Friday privilege loss, and under 20% item completion.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply matching-law efficiency principles (replacement behavior must require less effort and yield quicker payoff than problem behavior), FCT, DRA/DRI, and WWC K-5 behavioral guidance.

planningFrame.label: Intervention plan
planningFrame.guidance: Teach a laminated two-sided "Help / 2-Min Reset" card with immediate initial honor (under 20 seconds), remove timed-drill pressure, model fraction steps, and reinforce active tile use (DRI).

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Plan proactively for a temporary extinction burst, graph daily FCT requests vs. disruptions and math completion, and thin break frequency only after 80% stable mastery.

successCriteria: Designs an FCT replacement skill that is simpler, faster, and more reliably reinforced than profanity or sweeping tiles, directly resolving the 4-minute wait barrier.
Pairs DRA (reinforcing card use and math-step completion) and DRI (reinforcing hands-on structured tile use or self-checking) with withholding escape following disruption.
Addresses antecedent instructional friction (removing timed stress, pre-teaching fraction steps, chunking sets) so Brianna can experience genuine academic success.
Includes an explicit schedule-thinning sequence (introducing a visual wait timer and gradually raising completed problems per break) plus extinction-burst readiness.
commonPitfalls: Telling Brianna to "raise your hand and wait patiently" while keeping the 4-minute response delay that makes profanity far more efficient.
Honoring Brianna's FCT break card inconsistently or only after she has already started yelling, which chains escalation to escape.
Withholding reinforcement until Friday afternoon instead of delivering immediate, function-matched reinforcement during the math block.
Leaving Brianna permanently on unlimited breaks without a data-based thinning rule tied to math accuracy and tolerance for brief waits.
sampleOutline: FCT replacement design: Teach and rehearse a desk "Help / 2-Minute Reset" card during calm practice; honor requests within 15 seconds during acquisition so communication beats throwing tiles.

Antecedent & DRA/DRI pairing: Replace timed drills with 3-item chunked fraction strips and worked examples; reinforce appropriate tile manipulation and card use immediately while calmly prompting card use instead of rewarding profanity with task removal.
Extinction-burst preparation: Brief staff to remain calm, ensure safety, avoid lecturing, and reinforce the first appropriate request immediately if disruptions briefly spike.

Thinning & monitoring: Once disruptions drop to 1 or fewer weekly and card use is independent for 2 weeks, introduce a 1-minute visual wait timer and shift breaks to earned completion milestones while graphing daily math accuracy.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Replace Restrictive Door-Blocking with Trauma-Informed De-Escalation
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Design a phased acting-out cycle de-escalation protocol and legal-ethical safety plan for a seventh-grade student with EBD and complex trauma after staff nearly used an unauthorized physical restraint.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Malik (Grade 7, EBD with documented complex trauma) shows reliable early agitation cues—pulling his hood up, pacing near the back counter, jaw clenching, and muttering "back off"—4 to 6 minutes before overturning desks. Last week two untrained adults stepped between Malik and the door, gave rapid public ultimatums, touched his shoulder, and discussed a prone hold even though classmates had already exited and no one faced imminent physical harm.
taskParts: Analyze how adult crowding, doorway blocking, shoulder contact, and public ultimatums accelerated Malik's escalation through the acting-out cycle and conflicted with trauma-informed safety principles.
Build a phase-by-phase individualized crisis and de-escalation protocol covering calm, trigger, agitation, acceleration, peak, de-escalation, and recovery stages.

State the strict legal and ethical boundaries governing physical restraint and seclusion (including why prone restraint is prohibited), plus mandatory post-incident debriefing, documentation, and family notification.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Use Malik's 4-to-6-minute early warning window (hood up, pacing, clenched jaw) and the clear adult triggers (blocked exit, crowding, shoulder touch, rapid ultimatums) to anchor prevention.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply Colvin's acting-out cycle, trauma-informed co-regulation principles, U.S. Department of Education restraint/seclusion restraint-as-last-resort principles, and IDEA 34 CFR 300.530 BIP review duties.

planningFrame.label: Intervention plan
planningFrame.guidance: Designate one calm lead adult, preserve physical space and an unblocked safe-exit route, offer two low-demand regulation choices at agitation, clear peers at peak, and delay academic demands until recovery.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Prohibit prone/supine/mechanical restraints and punitive seclusion, restrict emergency physical holds strictly to imminent serious physical harm by certified staff, and mandate same-day family notice and IEP team BIP review.

successCriteria: Maps concrete staff actions to each phase of the acting-out cycle, focusing heavily on early agitation cues during the 4-to-6-minute prevention window.
Removes trauma triggers by establishing one calm speaker, non-threatening side posture, zero unsolicited touch, unblocked egress, and simple concrete choices.

Correctly states restraint and seclusion safeguards: emergency last resort only for imminent danger of serious physical harm, never for property destruction or noncompliance, never prone restraint, and never as a planned behavioral intervention.
Requires structured post-crisis recovery, restorative repair only after full physiological regulation, incident documentation, parent notification, and IEP team FBA/BIP updating.
commonPitfalls: Treating overturned desks or profanity alone as legal justification for physical restraint when peers are safe and no imminent bodily harm exists.
Trying to lecture, process emotions, or assign disciplinary consequences while Malik is still in peak or early de-escalation.
Allowing multiple adults to talk simultaneously, hover over Malik, or block the doorway to assert authority.
Writing emergency physical restraint into Malik's routine BIP as a standard consequence rather than strengthening proactive trauma-informed supports.
sampleOutline: Escalation audit: Blocking the doorway, touching Malik's shoulder, and firing public ultimatums triggered a trauma fight-or-flight response during his 4-to-6-minute agitation window.

Phased de-escalation protocol: At early agitation cues, one designated staff member lowers voice, gives 6 feet of space, leaves the exit clear, and offers a pre-agreed cool-down pass or silent walk; at peak, clear peers quietly and prioritize safety without arguing.

Restraint & seclusion boundaries: Enforce strict prohibition of prone holds and punitive seclusion; permit certified crisis intervention solely for imminent serious physical harm, never for property damage or defiance.

Recovery & system review: Allow quiet sensory recovery before brief restorative debriefing, notify Malik's caregiver immediately if any crisis protocol activates, train all Grade 7 staff, and reconvene the IEP team to update his BIP.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Break Task-Avoidance Writing Cycles Through SRSD and Self-Monitoring
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Design an integrated academic-behavioral intervention for a sixth-grade student with EBD whose persuasive-writing avoidance persisted despite a seat-time token economy.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Tessa (Grade 6, EBD with written-expression deficits) argues persuasively in oral class debates yet refuses English essays 4 of 5 days by dropping her head, debating rubric wording, and tearing drafts. Baseline probes show 18-word disorganized paragraphs with 0 counterarguments. A token chart rewarding "staying in seat" raised seat time to 86%, but written output stayed flat at 20 words and tearing episodes resumed once prompts grew longer.
taskParts: Explain the academic-behavior reciprocity breakdown demonstrated by Tessa's 86% seat time paired with flat 20-word drafts and resurgent draft-tearing.
Outline a Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) instructional sequence (such as POW+TREE) adapted to capitalize on Tessa's strong oral argumentation skills.
Pair SRSD with a student-operated self-monitoring, self-graphing, and positive feedback routine that promotes independent generalization across writing classes.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Contrast Tessa's strong oral debate skills and 86% token-driven seat time against her 18-to-20-word written baseline, 0 counterarguments, and 4-of-5-day essay avoidance.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply academic-behavior reciprocity principles, SRSD six-stage explicit strategy instruction, student self-monitoring/self-regulation research, and behavior-specific feedback standards.

planningFrame.label: Intervention plan
planningFrame.guidance: Shift reinforcement from passive compliance to strategy steps using SRSD (develop background, discuss, model with think-alouds, memorize POW+TREE, support with oral-to-text bridges, fade to independent performance).

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Have Tessa self-graph essay elements (topic, reasons, counterargument, ending) and total words written twice weekly while coaching frustration self-talk and checking fidelity across teachers.

successCriteria: Explains clearly why rewarding passive seat-time compliance failed: without explicit writing-strategy instruction, the underlying skill deficit continues to trigger escape and frustration.
Structures SRSD across its core instructional stages—including explicit teacher think-aloud modeling of both writing planning and coping self-statements before fading scaffolds.
Leverages Tessa's documented oral debate strength (such as oral rehearsal, speech-to-text planning, or graphic organizer dictation) as an instructional bridge to structured essays.
Incorporates student self-monitoring checklists and visual self-graphing of essay elements and quality rather than relying solely on adult-managed token points.
commonPitfalls: Tightening the seat-time token economy or deducting points for torn drafts without teaching an explicit essay-planning strategy.
Handing Tessa a graphic organizer worksheet and expecting independent use without modeling, guided practice, and mnemonic memorization.
Lowering the writing expectation to one-sentence fill-in-the-blank sheets instead of building Grade 6 persuasive structure from her oral debate strengths.
Measuring success only by quiet compliance rather than tracking essay elements, counterarguments, word count, and generalization to social studies.
sampleOutline: Reciprocity analysis: Tessa's 86% seat time with stagnant 20-word drafts proves compliance contingencies cannot solve a skill-based writing deficit; avoidance returns whenever essay length rises.

SRSD instructional plan: Teach POW+TREE through the six SRSD stages, beginning with oral debate-to-organizer bridges and explicit teacher think-alouds that model coping self-statements ("I can list two reasons first").

Self-monitoring & reinforcement: Replace passive seat tokens with a student checklist and bar graph tracking completed TREE elements, counterarguments, and calm help-seeking paired with behavior-specific praise.
Generalization & progress rules: Fade graphic prompts as Tessa hits 4 of 5 essay elements across 3 consecutive probes, then transfer the POW+TREE routine to Grade 6 social studies claims.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: ED eligibility vs. social maladjustment & MDR basis of knowledge
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Apply IDEA Emotional Disturbance Criteria and Basis-of-Knowledge Discipline Protections
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Resolve a high school eligibility and discipline dispute involving a ninth-grade student with chronic internalizing distress, recent truancy, and a proposed 12-day suspension while evaluation is pending.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Darius (Grade 9) has a 14-month record of persistent sadness, nurse visits for somatic headaches, peer withdrawal, and a GPA drop from 3.1 to 1.4. Last month his mother emailed the principal requesting an IDEA evaluation after two truancy citations and teacher referral logs. Before testing finished, Darius shoved a peer who mocked his family; a dean labels him "socially maladjusted" and proposes a 12-day suspension without an MDR.
taskParts: Distinguish IDEA Emotional Disturbance eligibility criteria from the social maladjustment exclusion using Darius's 14-month longitudinal data, explaining why truancy or a fight does not disqualify a student who also meets ED criteria.

Analyze why the school has a "basis of knowledge" under IDEA discipline regulations (34 CFR 300.534 / 300.530) despite Darius not yet having a finalized IEP, and identify the immediate procedural protections triggered.
Outline the required next steps for completing a nondiscriminatory multidisciplinary evaluation, conducting the MDR, and coordinating interim educational and mental-health supports.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Weigh the 14-month internalizing and academic trajectory (persistent sadness, somatic headaches, withdrawal, 3.1 to 1.4 GPA drop) alongside the mother's written evaluation email and teacher referral logs.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply federal Emotional Disturbance criteria (long period, marked degree, adverse educational effect, pervasive unhappiness/depression and physical symptoms/fears), the social maladjustment rule, and basis-of-knowledge MDR protections.

planningFrame.label: Intervention plan
planningFrame.guidance: Halt the unilateral 12-day removal without MDR, expedite the multidisciplinary evaluation, convene an MDR within 10 school days, and launch school counseling plus academic recovery supports.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Deliver Procedural Safeguards Notice immediately, guard against subjective bias in labeling externalizing anger as mere delinquency, and guarantee FAPE continuity if removal exceeds 10 days.

successCriteria: Accurately explains that IDEA excludes students who are socially maladjusted ONLY if they do not also meet Emotional Disturbance criteria—Darius's 14-month sadness, somatic symptoms, withdrawal, and GPA decline directly align with ED indicators.

Identifies that the mother's written evaluation request and documented teacher concerns establish IDEA "basis of knowledge," entitling Darius to full 34 CFR 300.530 MDR and change-of-placement protections.
Rejects the dean's unilateral 12-day suspension without MDR and notes the requirement for an expedited evaluation if requested during disciplinary action.

Recommends multimethod, culturally responsive evaluation (clinical/school interviews, multi-informant rating scales, observations, attendance/health records) paired with supportive trauma-sensitive interventions.
commonPitfalls: Accepting the dean's claim that two truancy citations and a hallway shove prove social maladjustment and automatically bar Emotional Disturbance eligibility.
Concluding Darius has zero IDEA discipline protections simply because his initial eligibility meeting has not happened yet.
Determining ED eligibility prematurely from a single checklist before completing a full multidisciplinary evaluation.
Overlooking somatic complaints and internalizing depression because the disciplinary incident involved a brief externalizing shove.
sampleOutline: ED vs. social maladjustment: IDEA excludes social maladjustment only absent Emotional Disturbance; Darius's 14-month depression, somatic headaches, withdrawal, and 3.1-to-1.4 GPA decline demonstrate chronic, marked adverse educational impact across multiple ED criteria.

Basis-of-knowledge safeguard: The mother's written evaluation request and staff referral logs establish district basis of knowledge, triggering full 34 CFR 300.530 protections against a 12-day suspension without an MDR.
Compliance sequence: Immediately issue Procedural Safeguards Notice, block unilateral removal beyond 10 days without a 10-school-day MDR, and complete an expedited multidisciplinary evaluation.
Supportive programming: Pair school-based mental health check-ins, safety planning around peer taunting, and targeted Grade 9 credit-recovery scaffolds with ongoing family collaboration.
