constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Coordinate a Strengths-Based Wraparound Re-Entry Plan Across Home, School, and Clinic
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Design a culturally responsive, legally compliant wraparound transition plan for an eighth-grade student with EBD returning from inpatient psychiatric stabilization amid fragmented agency communication.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Chloe (Grade 8, EBD) returns Monday after 3 weeks of inpatient psychiatric stabilization. Her grandmother (legal guardian) works two hourly shifts and avoids school meetings after blame-focused calls. Chloe sees an outpatient therapist, a psychiatrist adjusting morning medication causing first-period drowsiness, and a diversion caseworker, yet no releases exist and staff lack a CICO or makeup-work plan.
taskParts: Establish a legally compliant information-sharing and scheduling structure that respects FERPA/HIPAA signed releases, protects guardian confidentiality, and eliminates participation barriers for Chloe's grandmother.

Design a strengths-based wraparound re-entry plan connecting school Check-In/Check-Out (CICO), first-period medication-fatigue accommodations, phased academic catch-up, and shared early-warning safety cues.
Define clear interagency roles, generalization routines across home and school, and objective 30-day review metrics that monitor attendance, emotional safety, and caregiver trust.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Address every fragmentation point: 3-week psychiatric return, guardian's two hourly jobs and prior negative meetings, morning medication drowsiness, absent releases, and missing school CICO/makeup plan.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply wraparound family-voice and natural-support principles, FERPA and HIPAA reciprocal written-consent rules, IEP team re-entry review duties, and Tier 2/3 behavioral support fidelity.

planningFrame.label: Intervention plan
planningFrame.guidance: Offer flexible phone/evening planning with the grandmother, secure targeted two-way releases, launch soft-landing CICO with a trusted adult, adjust first-period demands, and align crisis triggers with the therapist.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Limit shared data to need-to-know educational/safety goals, ensure Chloe helps choose her trusted adult and coping tools, and review attendance, CICO points, and family feedback at Days 10 and 30.

successCriteria: Requires specific, informed written releases of information from Chloe's legal guardian (grandmother) before exchanging educational (FERPA) or clinical (HIPAA) records with outside providers.
Removes caregiver barriers through flexible meeting formats, strengths-first communication, and genuine shared decision-making rather than deficit-based reporting.

Addresses concrete re-entry needs directly: first-period medication drowsiness adjustments, prioritized essential makeup work instead of a punitive pileup, trusted-adult CICO, and aligned crisis safety steps.
Centers Chloe's own voice in selecting coping signals and tracks measurable 30-day re-entry indicators (attendance, CICO stability, safe pass use, and caregiver communication satisfaction).
commonPitfalls: Calling Chloe's outpatient therapist or psychiatrist to exchange behavioral details before obtaining signed written guardian releases.
Scheduling an inflexible mid-morning school meeting and documenting the grandmother as "uncooperative" when her hourly shifts prevent attendance.
Overwhelming Chloe on Day 1 with 3 weeks of unprioritized makeup worksheets or penalizing first-period drowsiness as defiance.
Sharing sensitive psychiatric hospitalization details broadly with all building staff instead of restricting need-to-know safety plans to designated IEP implementers.
sampleOutline: Family-centered engagement & privacy: Contact Chloe's grandmother with a strengths-based welcome, offer flexible early-morning/video/phone scheduling, and obtain targeted written FERPA/HIPAA releases before coordinating with her therapist, psychiatrist, and caseworker.

School re-entry scaffolding: Convene an IEP review to add a trusted-adult CICO routine, non-punitive first-period movement/check-in accommodations for medication fatigue, and a trimmed essential-standards makeup schedule.

Interagency alignment: Map one shared crisis/early-warning protocol with the outpatient clinician and Chloe so school staff recognize calming cues and know exact escalation contacts without over-sharing confidential clinical history.
Outcome & trust review: Track daily attendance, CICO regulation scores, safe-pass usage, and brief weekly positive guardian check-ins, reconvening the wraparound team at Days 10 and 30.
constructedResponseWorkshops.reviewNote: Independent applied case-analysis practice; not an official ETS prompt, rubric, score, pass prediction, or eligibility/licensure determination. AlloFlow does not score written responses.

quickReference.domainLabel: Development and Characteristics of Students with EBD
quickReference.title: IDEA Emotional Disturbance Criteria, Profiles & Trauma Context
quickReference.purpose: Anchors IDEA Emotional Disturbance eligibility gates, internalizing versus externalizing profiles, comorbidity, and trauma-informed developmental interpretation.
checklist: Verify duration, intensity, and adverse educational impact across multiple settings before attributing distress to Emotional Disturbance.
Screen for both externalizing behaviors (aggression, defiance, impulsivity) and easily overlooked internalizing signs (withdrawal, somatic complaints, chronic anxiety, depression).
Evaluate trauma history, cultural norms, language demands, academic skill gaps, and medical or medication factors that co-occur with emotional-behavioral needs.
formulas: IDEA Emotional Disturbance (ED) 5 characteristics (34 CFR 300.8(c)(4)): over a long period of time and to a marked degree that adversely affects educational performance, exhibiting one or more of (A) unexplained inability to learn, (B) inability to build/maintain satisfactory interpersonal relationships, (C) inappropriate behavior or feelings under normal circumstances, (D) general pervasive mood of unhappiness or depression, or (E) physical symptoms/fears tied to personal or school problems.

IDEA ED inclusion and exclusion rule: Emotional Disturbance explicitly includes schizophrenia, and explicitly excludes children who are socially maladjusted unless the team determines the child also meets Emotional Disturbance criteria.

Externalizing vs internalizing comorbidity: students with EBD frequently show co-occurring reading/writing deficits (SLD), ADHD, executive-function delays, and trauma-stress dysregulation; academic frustration frequently drives escape-maintained behavioral escalation.

Trauma-informed developmental lens: chronic adversity alters threat detection, emotional regulation, and stress physiology; prioritize predictability, relational safety, co-regulation, and skill building over punitive compliance demands.
decisionRules: When a student shows sudden school avoidance, headaches, tearfulness, and declining work completion over several months → prioritize screening for internalizing emotional distress and academic barriers rather than assuming defiance or laziness.

When an evaluation team argues a student cannot qualify for ED solely because conduct involves peer-group rule breaking → prioritize assessing whether underlying ED characteristics (depression, anxiety, pervasive relational impairment) coexist alongside social maladjustment.

When a student’s irritability and drowsiness shift sharply after a new psychotropic prescription → prioritize documenting objective behavioral frequency/time patterns and notifying parents/school nurse rather than adjusting or recommending medication.

When culturally expressive communication styles trigger repeated office referrals in one classroom but not others → prioritize examining teacher-student interaction patterns and cultural responsiveness before labeling the behavior disordered.
cautions: Never diagnose psychiatric disorders (such as bipolar disorder, conduct disorder, or PTSD) or advise families to start, stop, or alter psychotropic medications; educators document observable school functioning.
Do not overlook quiet, compliant students experiencing severe internalizing depression or anxiety when prioritizing behavioral supports.
Avoid equating a single crisis incident or short-term grief reaction with IDEA’s "over a long period of time and to a marked degree" ED criterion.

quickReference.domainLabel: Planning and Managing the Learning Environments
quickReference.title: SWPBIS Prevention, Acting-Out Cycle & Safe De-Escalation
quickReference.purpose: Anchors multi-tiered behavioral prevention, Colvin’s 7-phase Acting-Out Cycle, proactive classroom management, and trauma-safe de-escalation protocols.
checklist: Audit classroom antecedents first: clear 3 to 5 positively stated expectations, predictable transitions, physical traffic flow, and task-difficulty match.
Identify the student’s current phase on the Acting-Out Cycle before choosing verbal prompts, space, or instructional redirection.
Verify that Tier 2 and Tier 3 behavioral supports align with measurable IEP social-emotional goals and crisis safety plans.
formulas: SWPBIS three-tier prevention framework: Tier 1 universal expectations, active supervision, precorrection, and at least 4:1 to 5:1 behavior-specific praise-to-correction ratio; Tier 2 targeted Check-In/Check-Out (CICO), social skills groups, and self-monitoring; Tier 3 individualized FBA-based BIP and wraparound coordination.

Colvin’s 7-Phase Acting-Out Cycle: (1) Calm (teach/reinforce), (2) Trigger (prevent/redirect), (3) Agitation (reduce demands, offer choices/space), (4) Acceleration (stay calm, neutral tone, avoid power struggles), (5) Peak (safety only, clear peers, minimal speech), (6) De-escalation (cool-down, simple independent task), (7) Recovery (debrief, teach replacement skill, restore relationship).

Proactive antecedent strategies: precorrection before predictable problem routines, high-probability request sequences (3 easy requests before a low-probability demand), structured choices, environmental arrangement, and noncontingent reinforcement (NCR).

Contingency management systems: token economies (defined target behaviors, clear exchange schedule, backup reinforcers, systematic fading), Good Behavior Game (interdependent group contingency), and behavioral contracting (mutually negotiated criteria and rewards).
decisionRules: When a student enters the Agitation or Acceleration phase with clenched fists and raised voice → prioritize lowering vocal volume, giving physical space, offering two structured choices, and avoiding public confrontation or rapid-fire commands.

When a student reaches Peak crisis behavior posing immediate danger → prioritize student and peer physical safety with minimal verbal talk and activate the team crisis protocol, saving debriefing and problem-solving for the Recovery phase.

When classroom disruption clusters every day during the 5-minute transition from lunch to math → prioritize precorrection, explicit routine rehearsal, active supervision, and immediate behavior-specific praise for smooth entry.

When a Tier 2 student seeks adult attention and responds well to predictable daily feedback → prioritize Check-In/Check-Out (CICO) with brief morning goal setting, structured period ratings, and afternoon positive check-out.
cautions: Never attempt rational lecturing, consequence bargaining, or skill teaching during the Acceleration or Peak phases of the Acting-Out Cycle.
Do not use response cost or point-removal systems that strip previously earned tokens in ways that trigger explosive escalation or learned helplessness.
Avoid implementing physical seclusion or restraint as a routine consequence, convenience measure, or response to verbal disrespect without imminent serious physical harm.

quickReference.title: Academic Instruction, Social Skills, Self-Monitoring & Generalization
quickReference.purpose: Anchors high-leverage explicit academic instruction, behavioral skills training, cognitive-behavioral strategy instruction, and Stokes and Baer generalization rules.
checklist: Check whether task avoidance stems from an unaddressed reading, writing, or math skill gap (can’t do) rather than a motivational deficit (won’t do).
Pair every social-emotional or self-regulation skill lesson with modeling, role-play rehearsal, performance feedback, and natural-setting prompts.
Build explicit generalization and fading plans from the first day of instruction so skills transfer beyond the resource room.
formulas: High-engagement academic instruction for EBD: brisk pacing, high Opportunities to Respond (3 to 5 choral/response-card/partner prompts per minute), chunked assignments, errorless or scaffolded entry, and immediate affirmative/corrective feedback.

Behavioral Skills Training (BST) for social and self-advocacy skills: four sequential steps—(1) explicit instruction/rationale, (2) live or video modeling, (3) structured rehearsal/role-play, and (4) immediate specific feedback to mastery.

Cognitive-behavioral and strategy instruction: Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD: Develop background knowledge, Discuss, Model, Memorize, Support, Independent performance, such as POW+TREE for writing), self-monitoring (cue + self-recording + self-graphing), and self-instructional problem-solving scripts.

Stokes and Baer generalization technologies: train and hope fails; instead program common stimuli, train loosely across settings/partners, use multiple exemplars, reinforce naturally occurring communities of reinforcement, and teach self-mediated cues.
decisionRules: When a student tears up multi-paragraph writing prompts every afternoon → prioritize pairing explicit SRSD writing scaffolds (such as POW+TREE) with chunked milestones and break-request coaching rather than relying solely on behavioral penalties.

When a student demonstrates anger-management steps accurately during counseling role-play but still erupts in general-education hallways → prioritize programming common cues, training across multiple natural settings, and prompting general-education teachers to reinforce the replacement skill.

When an adolescent with EBD displays off-task fidgeting and incomplete assignments despite possessing the academic skill → prioritize teaching a discreet self-monitoring and self-graphing routine paired with periodic teacher accuracy checks.

When group discussions stall because students with EBD hesitate to risk public mistakes → prioritize simultaneous high-OTR strategies (dry-erase boards, response cards, think-pair-share) to raise engagement and lower social threat.
cautions: Never rely on "train and hope" pull-out social skills lessons without embedding prompts and reinforcement in general-education classrooms and peer settings.
Do not deliver watered-down busywork to keep students calm; academic under-challenge and skill gaps both accelerate long-term EBD disengagement.
Avoid skipping error correction or letting a student practice an incorrect academic or social response repeatedly without supportive modeling.

quickReference.title: Direct Observation Systems, FBA Functions & BIP Design
quickReference.purpose: Anchors operational definitions, direct behavioral recording formulas, four-function FBA analysis, and functionally matched Behavior Intervention Plans.
checklist: Write an observable, measurable operational definition of the target behavior (passes the dead-man and stranger tests) before collecting baseline data.
Match the recording method to the behavior’s physical dimension (discrete count, episode length, start delay, or continuous rate).
Verify the hypothesized behavioral function across indirect interviews, direct ABC observation, and scatterplots before selecting BIP interventions.
formulas: Direct behavioral measurement selection: Event/Frequency recording for discrete, uniform-length behaviors; Duration recording for how long episodes last; Latency recording for time between directive and initiation; Whole-Interval recording (underestimates) for continuous skills to increase; Partial-Interval recording (overestimates) for high-rate behaviors to decrease; Momentary Time Sampling (unbiased snapshot at interval end) for classroom multitasking.

FBA four behavioral functions and ABC logic: Antecedent (setting events + immediate triggers) → Behavior (observable topography) → Consequence (maintaining reinforcer): Escape/Avoidance, Attention (peer or adult), Access to Tangibles/Activities, or Automatic/Sensory reinforcement.

Competing Behavior Pathway and replacement criteria: a Functional Replacement Behavior (such as Functional Communication Training, FCT) must serve the EXACT same function as the problem behavior while being equal or lower in effort and equal or faster in reinforcement efficiency.

Differential reinforcement selection: DRA (reinforce a functionally equivalent alternative), DRI (reinforce a physically incompatible behavior), DRO (reinforce absence of problem behavior for a set interval), and Extinction (withhold maintaining reinforcer—anticipate an initial extinction burst and never use alone for dangerous behavior).
decisionRules: When a student throws pencils during independent math and is repeatedly sent to the hallway (escape function) → prioritize teaching an FCT break or help request, modifying task entry, and avoiding escape-reinforcing exclusionary removals.

When a teacher wants to track continuous on-task seatwork while teaching a full class of 24 students → prioritize Momentary Time Sampling at 2- to 5-minute intervals rather than continuous duration recording.

When baseline ABC data show disruptive jokes occur only during unstructured partner time and reliably draw peer laughter → prioritize peer-attention-matched DRA/DRI (structured leadership or earned peer-sharing time) plus teaching peers to reinforce on-task contributions.

When a newly launched extinction component causes a brief spike in screaming intensity during days 1 to 3 → prioritize maintaining safety and heavy reinforcement of the replacement behavior, recognizing a predictable extinction burst rather than immediately abandoning the BIP.
cautions: Never use time-out or hallway removal for an escape-maintained behavior, because removal negatively reinforces the exact target behavior you want to reduce.
Do not design a BIP around topography (what the behavior looks like) instead of function (what consequence maintains it).
Avoid using partial-interval recording to prove a student stayed on task for 90% of class, since partial-interval systematically overestimates continuous duration.

quickReference.title: IDEA Discipline, MDR, Restrictive Safeguards & Interagency Care
quickReference.purpose: Anchors IDEA disciplinary protections, Honig v. Doe stay-put, restraint/seclusion ethical limits, equity disproportionality checks, and wraparound collaboration.
checklist: Track cumulative suspension days (including informal "sent home early" removals and bus suspensions that prevent attendance) against the 10-school-day threshold.
Confirm informed parental written consent before exchanging confidential student mental-health or juvenile-justice records with outside agencies.
Verify that crisis interventions prioritize least-restrictive de-escalation and meet federal/state documentation and parent-notification rules.
formulas: Honig v. Doe (1988) and IDEA 10-day rule (34 CFR 300.530): schools may not unilaterally exclude a student with a disability for more than 10 consecutive school days (or a pattern of removals exceeding 10 cumulative days) without an MDR within 10 school days and continued FAPE services starting on day 11.

MDR two-prong legal test and remedies: (1) was conduct caused by or directly/substantially related to the disability, OR (2) was conduct the direct result of LEA failure to implement the IEP? If Yes to either, conduct/review FBA and BIP and return student to placement (unless 45-school-day IAES applies for weapons, drugs, or serious bodily injury, or parent/LEA agree to change).

Protections for not-yet-eligible students (34 CFR 300.534): IDEA discipline protections apply if the LEA had "basis of knowledge" prior to the incident (parent expressed concern in writing, parent requested evaluation, or teacher/staff expressed specific concerns about a pattern of behavior to supervisory staff).

Restraint, seclusion, and wraparound ethics (CEC / USDOE 15 Principles): physical restraint or seclusion is restricted strictly to imminent danger of serious physical harm, never prone/mechanical/chemical restraint or punishment, requires immediate parent notice and debriefing; interagency wraparound integrates family voice, school mental health, and community clinicians under signed releases.
decisionRules: When an MDR team finds that staff repeatedly failed to deliver the student’s BIP check-ins before an office outburst → prioritize ruling the behavior a manifestation under Prong 2, immediately remedying IEP/BIP implementation, and returning the student to placement.

When an administrator calls a parent weekly to pick up an agitated student with EBD for the afternoon without logging formal suspensions → prioritize documenting these informal removals toward the 10-day FAPE/change-of-placement count and convening the IEP team to revise behavioral supports.

When a student not yet receiving special education brings a pocketknife to school one week after the parent submitted a written evaluation request → prioritize applying full IDEA basis-of-knowledge discipline protections and an expedited evaluation.

When disaggregated discipline data reveal Black or Indigenous students with EBD receive out-of-school suspensions at triple the rate of peers for subjective "defiance" referrals → prioritize reviewing referral definitions, implicit bias, and restorative/PBIS alternatives at the systems level.
cautions: Never treat "serious bodily injury" under the 45-school-day IAES rule loosely; statutory definition (18 USC 1365(h)(3)) requires substantial risk of death, extreme physical pain, protracted disfigurement, or protracted loss of bodily function—not ordinary scrapes or bruises.

Do not share IEP or behavioral logs with an outside therapist, probation officer, or physician without a signed, time-limited FERPA release (unless a documented imminent health/safety emergency exists).
Avoid blaming families for a student’s emotional-behavioral challenges; frame family collaboration around shared strengths, ecological context, and mutual trust.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Intervening on Behavior Topography Instead of FBA-Identified Function
misconceptionFamilies.description: Selecting behavior interventions based on what a disruptive behavior looks like (such as shouting, tearing paper, or walking out) rather than analyzing Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence (ABC) data to identify the maintaining function (escape/avoidance, attention, tangible access, or automatic sensory stimulation).
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Always identify the hypothesized function from ABC patterns before choosing a consequence: removing a student who acts out to escape difficult math tasks negatively reinforces the problem behavior, whereas teaching an appropriate escape/help request paired with antecedent task supports breaks the cycle.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Confusing DRA, DRI, DRO, and Functional Communication Training (FCT)
misconceptionFamilies.description: Mixing up differential reinforcement procedures (DRA, DRI, DRO, DRL) or attempting planned ignoring and extinction without teaching a functionally equivalent, lower-effort replacement response through Functional Communication Training (FCT).
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Match the differential reinforcement procedure to the exact behavioral goal (DRA reinforces an appropriate alternative serving the same function, DRI reinforces a physically incompatible behavior, DRO reinforces absence of the target behavior over an interval) and pair extinction with immediate FCT reinforcement so the replacement beats the problem behavior in effort and speed.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Escalating Crisis Cycles or Misusing Seclusion and Restraint as Behavior Plans
misconceptionFamilies.description: Using verbal confrontation, public reprimands, or academic problem-solving during the agitation, acceleration, or peak phases of Colvin's acting-out cycle, or embedding physical restraint and seclusion as routine BIP consequences rather than last-resort emergency safety measures.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Align adult response to the exact acting-out phase (quiet prompts and choices in agitation; calm space, minimal talk, and safety clearance at peak; non-punitive debriefing only in recovery) and restrict physical restraint or seclusion strictly to imminent risk of serious physical harm by trained staff with immediate documentation, parent notification, and post-incident review.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Overlooking Internalizing EBD and Trauma Responses as Willful Defiance
misconceptionFamilies.description: Associating Emotional and Behavioral Disorders exclusively with loud externalizing conduct while missing severe anxiety, depression, somatic complaints, and social withdrawal, or misinterpreting trauma-triggered hyperarousal and IDEA's social-maladjustment exclusion clause.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Screen systematically for internalizing distress alongside externalizing behaviors, apply IDEA's five Emotional Disturbance criteria (requiring duration, marked degree, and adverse educational impact, while recognizing that students with social maladjustment still qualify if they also have an emotional disturbance), and respond to trauma triggers with predictable safety routines and cognitive-behavioral coping supports.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Separating Behavior Control from Explicit Academic and Self-Management Instruction
misconceptionFamilies.description: Withholding rigorous grade-level instruction until behavior is fully compliant, ignoring academic skill deficits that trigger escape-maintained outbursts, or keeping students permanently dependent on teacher-run token economies without fading into self-monitoring and social-skills generalization.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Pair proactive academic supports (high opportunities to respond, behavior-specific praise at a 4:1 positive-to-corrective ratio, chunked tasks, precorrection) with explicit cognitive-behavioral self-management (self-monitoring, self-evaluation, self-reinforcement) and coached generalization across classrooms.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Selecting Mismatched Behavioral Recording Systems or Neglecting BIP Fidelity in MDR
misconceptionFamilies.description: Using event (frequency) recording for continuous or indistinct behaviors instead of duration, latency, or interval sampling, or evaluating disciplinary removals without verifying whether the student's BIP was implemented with fidelity before blaming the student.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Match the direct-observation metric to the target dimension (frequency/rate for discrete countable acts, duration for episode length, latency for start delay, whole-interval for behaviors to increase, partial-interval for behaviors to decrease, momentary time sampling for classroom on-task checks) and audit BIP implementation fidelity during every progress review and MDR.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Intervening on Behavior Topography Instead of FBA-Identified Function
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Trace ABC Contingencies to Function Before Designing Any BIP Intervention
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A 5372 vignette describes a student who curses, throws books, or leaves the room during independent writing, and a tempting distractor recommends sending the student to the office or hallway time-out.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: What happens immediately after the behavior in the ABC data—does the student gain attention/tangibles or escape an aversive demand—and would the proposed consequence accidentally reinforce that exact function?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Separate the behavior's topography (what it looks like) from its ABC pattern (setting event → immediate antecedent → behavior → maintaining consequence) and check whether any answer choice hands the student the exact outcome maintaining the behavior.
stages.requiredOutput: State the hypothesized behavioral function (escape, attention, tangible, or automatic) and identify which distractor unintentionally reinforces it.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Build a three-part competing-behavior pathway aligned to function: antecedent modification (prevent the trigger), functionally equivalent replacement behavior (teach an easier way to get the same outcome), and consequence shift (reinforce the replacement while discontinuing reinforcement of the target behavior).
stages.requiredOutput: Write one antecedent change, one replacement skill, and one consequence change for an escape-maintained work-refusal pattern.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Compare two students who both flip desks: Student A flips desks only during timed reading aloud and is sent to the counselor's office; Student B flips desks during quiet seatwork and peers laugh while the teacher lectures for five minutes.
stages.requiredOutput: Contrast the maintaining function for Student A (negative reinforcement via task escape) versus Student B (positive reinforcement via peer/adult attention) and prescribe a distinct BIP move for each.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-read a 5372 FBA case where an FBA hypothesis is tested across settings, then pick the first intervention step aligned to the ABC summary statement.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose the function-matched antecedent and replacement intervention while eliminating topography-driven punitive time-out choices.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Confusing DRA, DRI, DRO, and Functional Communication Training (FCT)
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Select the Exact Differential Reinforcement Schedule and Pair Extinction with FCT
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: An item contrasts DRA, DRI, DRO, DRL, and FCT, or proposes planned ignoring alone for a high-intensity attention-seeking or escape-maintained behavior without teaching a replacement request.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Which exact behavioral relationship is being reinforced (same-function alternative, physically incompatible act, or zero-occurrence interval), and have we taught a faster, lower-effort communicative replacement?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect the intervention mechanics in each answer choice to see whether it targets a physically incompatible action (DRI), a functionally equivalent alternative (DRA/FCT), total absence of the behavior during an interval (DRO), or reduced rate (DRL), and flag extinction-only choices that invite an extinction burst.
stages.requiredOutput: Label the reinforcement schedule shown in the stem and flag any distractor that uses extinction without teaching a replacement behavior.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Distinguish DRA (such as raising a hand or tapping a break card instead of calling out), DRI (such as keeping hands folded in lap, which is physically impossible while hitting), DRO (reinforcing every 5-minute interval free of profanity regardless of what else occurs), and FCT (explicitly teaching and immediately honoring a communicative request matched to the FBA function before gradually thinning the schedule).
stages.requiredOutput: Write a concise 4-row rule differentiating DRA, DRI, DRO, and FCT, including one classroom example and one common pitfall for each.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Design the FCT and differential reinforcement plan for a seventh grader who shouts insults to obtain a 2-minute break from lengthy writing tasks, deciding how to prompt the replacement break card, honor it initially on a dense schedule, and handle an initial extinction burst.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify the exact DRA/FCT response, initial continuous reinforcement schedule, extinction safety check, and systematic thinning rule.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Solve a fresh 5372 item asking which differential reinforcement procedure best reduces out-of-seat wandering by reinforcing seated task completion.
stages.requiredOutput: Select DRI (seated work is physically incompatible with out-of-seat wandering) and justify why DRO or punishment alone is less precise.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Escalating Crisis Cycles or Misusing Seclusion and Restraint as Behavior Plans
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Match De-Escalation to the Acting-Out Cycle and Enforce Restraint Safety Limits
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A student is visibly escalating (pacing, clenched fists, yelling) or in crisis peak, and distractors suggest lecturing about rules, issuing ultimatums, blocking exits, or writing seclusion/restraint into a proactive BIP.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Which phase of Colvin's acting-out cycle is the student in right now, and does the proposed adult move reduce arousal and protect physical safety without unlawfully using restraint or seclusion for noncompliance?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Locate the student's exact stage on the 7-phase acting-out cycle (Calm → Trigger → Agitation → Acceleration → Peak → De-escalation → Recovery) and spot adult escalators (raised voice, hovering, public power struggles, premature processing) or unlawful restraint triggers (property damage without bodily danger, verbal defiance).
stages.requiredOutput: Name the current crisis phase and flag any distractor that either escalates confrontation or violates restraint/seclusion emergency criteria.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Pair each crisis phase with its evidence-based staff action: Calm (teach coping skills), Trigger/Agitation (empathy, space, two structured choices, low-demand redirection), Acceleration (step back, calm neutral tone, pause verbal debating), Peak (focus solely on immediate physical safety, clear bystanders, summon trained crisis team), De-escalation (simple independent calming task, no lecturing), Recovery (supportive debrief and problem-solving); reserve physical restraint strictly for imminent danger of serious physical harm with continuous monitoring, immediate parent notice, written report, and BIP review.
stages.requiredOutput: Map the adult priority for Agitation, Peak, and Recovery, and list the three mandatory legal/ethical conditions governing emergency physical restraint.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Sequence the teacher's actions when a high school student with EBD slams a laptop shut, paces rapidly near the door, and mutters threats after receiving a low quiz grade—contrasting what to do immediately versus after the student calms down 20 minutes later.
stages.requiredOutput: Detail the low-arousal Agitation response (space, neutral voice, brief choice of quiet corner or nurse/counselor pass) and delay restorative problem-solving until the Recovery phase.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Evaluate a new 5372 ethics item where a team considers adding a locked quiet room to a student's BIP for repeated refusal to follow directions.
stages.requiredOutput: Reject seclusion as a planned consequence for noncompliance and select proactive antecedent supports, FBA/BIP revision, and emergency-only safety protocols.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Overlooking Internalizing EBD and Trauma Responses as Willful Defiance
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Identify Internalizing EBD, Trauma Triggers, and IDEA Social-Maladjustment Nuances
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A vignette features a quiet student with frequent nurse visits, perfectionistic shutdowns, flat affect, or sudden panic after loud hallway transitions—or tests whether a student with conduct problems can ever qualify under IDEA Emotional Disturbance.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Are we screening for covert internalizing distress and trauma-informed safety needs rather than reacting only to overt disruption, and how does IDEA's social-maladjustment clause actually work?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Scan the vignette for internalizing indicators (withdrawal, somatic complaints, excessive worry, self-deprecation, school avoidance), trauma-linked fight/flight/freeze cues, and legal traps claiming any student with conduct disorder is automatically excluded from IDEA.
stages.requiredOutput: Classify the presentation as internalizing, externalizing, or mixed, and flag any misconception about willful defiance or blanket social-maladjustment exclusion.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Review IDEA's Emotional Disturbance definition (at least one of five characteristics over a long period of time, to a marked degree, adversely affecting educational performance; includes schizophrenia; excludes socially maladjusted students ONLY if they do not also exhibit an emotional disturbance) and connect internalizing/trauma profiles to multi-gate screening (such as SRSS-IE) and trauma-informed predictability.
stages.requiredOutput: State the three duration/severity/impact qualifiers for IDEA Emotional Disturbance and explain the exact legal boundary of the social-maladjustment exclusion.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Analyze two students: (1) a quiet eighth grader whose grades drop sharply alongside daily stomachaches, tearfulness, and avoidance of group work; (2) a student in foster care who bolts from the classroom whenever a teacher raises their voice unexpectedly.
stages.requiredOutput: Recommend systematic internalizing screening and CBT/coping-skill IEP supports for student 1, and trauma-informed antecedent predictability, safe-space signal, and co-regulation routines for student 2.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-read a 5372 characteristics item asking why girls and quiet students with depression or anxiety are historically under-identified for EBD services.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the explanation centered on referral bias toward overt classroom disruption and endorse universal multi-informant screening that captures internalizing symptoms.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Separating Behavior Control from Explicit Academic and Self-Management Instruction
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Integrate High-Engagement Instruction with Self-Monitoring and Generalization
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: An instructional item either postpones core curriculum until behavior improves, ignores frustrational-level work triggering outbursts, or relies permanently on teacher-delivered tokens without building student self-regulation.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Is the instructional plan actively preventing behavior through matched task difficulty and high engagement while systematically transferring behavioral control from the teacher to the student?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Check whether the scenario's behavioral flare-ups coincide with academic frustration, low rates of active responding, or teacher-dependent reinforcement systems that collapse the moment the student enters a general education room.
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the missing academic-engagement lever or self-management generalization bridge in the scenario.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Connect evidence-based instructional prevention (interspersing known and new items, behavioral momentum, high opportunities to respond, 4:1 behavior-specific praise, guided notes) to the four-step self-management transfer sequence (teach target definition → student self-monitors with cue → accuracy match with teacher → fade external tokens while practicing across settings).
stages.requiredOutput: Explain how high-probability request sequences and student self-monitoring reduce escape-maintained disruption and promote cross-classroom generalization.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Redesign a sixth-grade inclusion social studies block where a student with EBD earns teacher-tracked points in the resource room but refuses work and argues during 25-minute silent reading in general education.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify two instructional modifications/scaffolds (chunked guided reading with high-p momentum and choice of response mode) plus a self-monitoring checklist faded from 5-minute intervals to end-of-period check-ins.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Solve a fresh 5372 instruction item asking how to ensure a newly taught anger-management or social-skills strategy actually transfers from a small counseling group into lunchroom and hallway conflicts.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose natural-setting practice, peer/adult prompting cues, and self-evaluation across multiple exemplars rather than isolated worksheet discussions.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Selecting Mismatched Behavioral Recording Systems or Neglecting BIP Fidelity in MDR
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Choose Exact Direct-Observation Metrics and Verify BIP Fidelity Before Placement Changes
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: An assessment item gives a target behavior—such as tantrum length, time to start work, or continuous humming—and asks for the best recording method, OR proposes a more restrictive placement without checking whether the current BIP was implemented consistently.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Which exact behavioral dimension (count, length, start delay, or interval estimate) matches the target behavior, and do we have fidelity data proving the BIP was actually delivered before altering placement?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect the operational definition of the behavior for four clues: clear start/end boundaries, high versus low frequency, time-until-initiation, or continuous duration—and check whether adult implementation fidelity was measured.
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the target behavioral dimension and flag any recording tool that distorts that dimension (such as frequency counting for continuous off-task staring).

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Match each recording method to its exact measurement property: Event/Frequency (discrete, countable acts of uniform length), Rate (frequency divided by observation time when session lengths vary), Duration (how long an episode lasts), Latency (time from teacher directive to compliance start), Partial-Interval (best for behaviors to decrease; may overestimate), Whole-Interval (best for behaviors to increase; may underestimate), Momentary Time Sampling (practical for busy classrooms checking on-task engagement).
stages.requiredOutput: Match five EBD classroom behaviors (swearing, crying episodes, starting math after cue, sustained seatwork, rocking) to their single most accurate recording system.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Audit a case where a ninth grader with EBD is recommended for a separate day school after three weeks on a new BIP, yet classroom logs show the check-in/check-out mentor met only twice and teachers delivered breaks inconsistently.
stages.requiredOutput: Explain why low treatment integrity invalidates calling the BIP ineffective, specify how to measure BIP fidelity directly, and outline the MDR prong-2 implication if disciplinary removals occurred.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Evaluate a new 5372 progress-monitoring vignette requiring selection of an interval sampling method for a high-rate continuous vocalization during 30-minute ELA blocks.
stages.requiredOutput: Select partial-interval recording (or momentary time sampling when teaching simultaneously) and explain why raw frequency counts would be unreliable.
